description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation. Carolyn Lazard (b. 1987) is a New York-based artist whose primary medium is iteration. They also work across video, sculpture, installation, and performance. Their practice remembers the generative incapacity of debility. Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is organized by the Cantor Arts Center, presenting work originally co-commissioned by the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis; the Institute of Contemporary Art, University of Pennsylvania; and Nottingham Contemporary, and is curated by Christina Linden, Director of Academic and Public Programs. We gratefully acknowledge support from The Lynn Krywick Gibbons Gallery Exhibitions Fund at the Cantor Arts Center.
title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take

description: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection showcases recent acquisitions made through the Cantor’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI), offering a glimpse into one of the fastest-growing areas of the museum’s collection. Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time. Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art. What began with approximately 30 works by Asian American artists has grown to more than 800 through acquisitions, exhibitions, publications, archival research, and community collaboration. Rather than presenting a single definition of Asian American art, In Focus highlights its remarkable breadth. Spanning generations, media, and artistic approaches, the exhibition brings together works by artists of Asian descent working in the United States whose practices reflect a wide range of histories, perspectives, and creative concerns. Featuring works by Pacita Abad, Ching Ho Cheng, Tseng Kwong Chi, Young Joon Kwak, Masami Teraoka, and Rupy C. Tut, among others. description: In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year — a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Emergent Properties brings together a selection of highlights from deep within the collections of the David Rumsey Map Center: items that have not only proven to be rare or beautiful, but have become the drivers of scholarship, programming, and support areas that have resonated with our users. The forty objects in this exhibition represent these emergent properties. Though only a glimpse into the full breadth of the Center’s holdings, they reflect what has mattered most over the past ten years. description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation, deepening our understanding of this overlooked chapter in the history of art and technology. description: Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970 , acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction. This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman , Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson , Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope. A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.
title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford

description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other. This exhibition inhabits that intersection, where historic technologies of encoding meet their digital descendants. Printmaking and weaving become contact zones between traditional craft techniques and computational processes, recording and recoding gestures across media: photographs compressed and reassembled as strips, atomized prints woven into textile, and thrown clay fused with digitally printed forms. Where does resistance live in a material, and how do we encounter it? How do different materials choreograph their maker’s creative gestures through this resistance? As creative workflows migrate into digital space, something of that friction transforms. Tangling the Digital asks what becomes possible when that resistance is embraced rather than engineered away. A working loom lives in the gallery, bearing witness to the evolution of craft as weavings unfurl over the course of the exhibition. Together, the works invite visitors to locate the human body—as maker, as observer—in what they see. On View: September 29–December 4, 2026 Coulter Art Gallery, 355 Roth Way Gallery Hours: Monday–Friday, 1–5pm Opening Reception: Thursday, Oct. 1, 4–6pm Curated by Vanessa Chang FACULTY ARTISTS: Camille Utterback Hideo Mabuchi STUDENT ARTISTS: Navya Agarwal Calla Bai Kelsey Chen Rosemary Jiang Jiayi Luo Skylar Sledd Sarah Teaw ACKNOWLEDGMENTS Tangling the Digital is made possible by generous support from the MacArthur Foundation, Funding Good Chaos, the Department of Art and Art History, the Stanford Arts Institute, the Product Realization Lab, CESTA, and the Silicon Valley Archives. description: Overview This activity reviews current, evidence-based management of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): diagnosis and confirmatory testing, baseline risk stratification and staging, treatment targets and assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid, second-line PPAR agonist therapy with seladelpar and elafibranor, and management of pruritus, fatigue, and other extrahepatic manifestations. Through case-based audience polling and expert review of recent trial data, participants will be prepared to identify high-risk patients earlier and intensify therapy to improve long-term outcomes. description: Session Description: Join Dr. Simukai Chigudu for a book talk on Chasing Freedom: a story of being born in postcolonial Zimbabwe, shaped by his family's buried trauma of war and liberation. It is a moving account of a generation still searching for the freedom they were promised. Dr. Simukai Chigudu’s Chasing Freedom : Coming of Age at the End of Empire is a candid, emotionally resonant exploration of family, nation, and the promises and limits of liberation. Drawing on his own life, Dr. Chigudu reconstructs a family shaped by struggle: a grandfather killed by the Rhodesian regime, a father who endured imprisonment and later fought as a guerrilla, and a mother who broke social constraints to support other women. Yet his upbringing was also suffused with British cultural practices, singing English folk songs, reading Shakespeare, and playing cricket, setting the stage for a disorienting culture shock when, in 2002, he left Zimbabwe for a boarding school in northern England. The book traces how historical violence, migration, and education reconfigure identity and belonging, and how a new generation continues to seek the freedom imagined by earlier movements. With scholarly rigor and humane storytelling, Dr. Chigudu offers a moving account of inherited trauma, resilience, and the complex legacies of empire, prompting reflection on both personal healing and public memory. About the Speaker Simukai Chigudu is an associate professor of African politics at the University of Oxford and a fellow of St Antony’s College. He was previously a fellow at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University. His academic monograph, The Political Life of an Epidemic: Cholera, Crisis and Citizenship in Zimbabwe (Cambridge University Press, 2020), received the 2021 APSA-IPSA Theodore J. Lowi First Book Award. He holds a DPhil in International Development from the University of Oxford, and his doctoral thesis received the 2018 Audrey Richards Prize, a biennial award presented by the African Studies Association of the United Kingdom for the best doctoral thesis in African Studies examined at a UK institution. Before entering academia, he worked as a medical doctor in the NHS for three years. He was also one of the founding members of Rhodes Must Fall in Oxford, and has become a leading voice in public debates on the cultural politics of colonialism and racism. Chasing Freedom is his first trade book.

Koyré, discovering that Galileo and Descartes both moved in parallel towards the discovery of the law of free fall – but that only Galileo made it – used this to identify Galileo’s originality as the first to form the specifically dynamic concepts of modern physics. description: Planetary atmospheres - and their potential habitability - evolve under external energy inputs, including stellar irradiation, cosmic rays, and meteoroid accretion. Meteoroid entry is ubiquitous across planetary systems but its role as a driver of atmospheric chemical evolution remains relatively underexplored. Meteorites readily acquire high entry velocities through planetary gravitational focusing, generating strong shock waves in planetary atmospheres during the entry process. The resulting shock heating drives non-equilibrium chemical reactions that can alter atmospheric compositions. We investigate these processes using coupled aerodynamical and chemical kinetic simulations of meteoroid entry. Our results demonstrate that meteoritic heating can significantly contribute to the production of organic species. Compared with other external energy sources such as stellar irradiation and cosmic rays, meteoroid entry processes have received relatively limited attention in atmospheric chemistry studies. Our results suggest that unlike stellar irradiation, which is primarily absorbed in the upper atmosphere, meteoroids can directly deposit energy into deeper atmospheric layers where most of the atmospheric mass resides. This enables shock-induced chemistry to proceed efficiently in dense atmospheric regions. Therefore, meteoritic heating may be a major contributor to chemical production in planetary atmospheres. Dr. Ryushi Miyayama is a postdoctoral scholar in Earth and Planetary Sciences under the supervision of Prof. Laura Schaefer. He received his Ph.D. in Physics from Nagoya University in 2026. During his Ph.D., he also worked with Prof. Schaefer on the physics and chemistry of planetary atmospheres, particularly how impacts and meteoroid entry drive atmospheric evolution. His recent work investigates shock-driven nonequilibrium chemistry during meteoroid entry into Titan’s atmosphere and its implications for the production of prebiotic molecules. Suggested reading: Ryushi Miyayama et al 2025 ApJ 989 210, https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/1538-4357/adf064
title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Ryushi Miyayama - "Atmospheric chemical evolution driven by meteoritic interactions"

description: Join the Fiber Optics Research Workshop in welcoming Professor Jacob Eyferth (University of Chicago) to Stanford Campus. Professor Eyferth will give a presentation entitled 'Sensing Nankeen: Skilled Perception as an Alternative to Centralized Production.' The Jiangnan cotton industry, centered on Songjiang (today part of Shanghai), was one of the largest industries of the eighteenth century in terms of volume and employment. Jiangnan cotton cloth, known in Europe as nankeen , was produced in millions of small household workshops and collected by traveling merchants who toured the countryside by boat and bought cloth in small batches, for further processing in urban workshops. Buying cloth required sensory skills: as Qianlong-periond training manuals explain, a skilled “cloth viewer” had to be able to assess the quality – the weight, density, color, etc. – of a bolt of cloth at first sight; moreover, he would know, by viewing and touching it, where, when, and how it was produced, with what tools, and from what raw materials. Most importantly, he could predict how the cloth would change under the dyers’ hands: cloth that looked smooth and clean might turn into stiff like felt in the vat, while cloth that looked less impressive would gain luster. Rather than seeking to standardize production, Songjiang cloth merchants embraced variety: all cloth, good or bad, had its use; even the coarsest cloth would find a market. The merchant’s task was to match product to market, using his body as scale and yardstick. The talk reconstructs cloth viewers’ embodied techniques as described in the Bu Jing 布经 training manual, asks to which extend skilled vision was, or could have been, an alternative to standardization and mass production, and looks at sensory training in Mao-era textile factories. This event is sponsored by Fiber Optics: Plant Fiber Materials & Media , a Research Workshop hosted by the Stanford Humanities Center, with support from the Center for East Asian Studies. Please RSVP for this event HERE .
title: Sensing Nankeen: Skilled Perception as an Alternative to Centralized Production

description: Expanding upon the work begun in What Tech Calls Thinking , Adrian Daub explores which ideas of politics, power, and dominance characterize the tech industry, and how those ideas came to be. Tech companies increasingly determine who regulates and who governs. And the tech elite increasingly wield political power, seeking to remake your workplace, your child's school, and the federal government in their image. But what do they mean by power? Taking readers from investor meetings to lecture halls, from science fiction to a neo-feudal worldview, Daub acerbically explores how tech culture approaches hierarchy and dominance, and what role a very specific form of masculinity plays in tech culture's ethos. From billboards to social media, Daub interrogates the way the tech elite exert power in their families and offices, but also in gyms and on YouTube channels, in courtrooms and on their commutes. As What Tech Calls Governing shows, to ask "how do they seek to dominate?" is actually to retell the history of Silicon Valley as the story of a fragile—and precisely for that reason domineering—masculinity intent on all the influence with none of the responsibility. Adrian Daub is J.E. Wallace Sterling Professor in the Humanities at Stanford University, where he serves as the Faculty Director of the Clayman Institute for Gender Research. He is the author of What Tech Calls Thinking (2020) and The Cancel Culture Panic (2024), and writes for numerous US and European newspapers and magazines.

description: Why do some backsliding incumbents co-opt civil society while others fail? This paper introduces a theory of civic consciousness, contending that, as compared to their formal or political counterparts, informal and apolitical civil society groups often fail to recognize their civic resources. I show that government threats to associational freedom help these groups recognize their latent social capital and increase their willingness to mobilize in support of democracy. As evidence, this paper draws on original data comprising the universe of Polish civil society between 2011 and 2025, a prominent period of democratic erosion and partial recovery. I find that Poland's illiberal PiS government financially targeted formal opposition groups but spared informal, apolitical groups. Meanwhile, those groups developed increased agency, leading them to avoid optional government interactions during the backsliding period. An original civil society-level survey experiment confirms that, when facing government threats, informal and apolitical groups are more likely to engage in pro-democratic actions. Altogether, I illustrate how improved civic consciousness facilitates newfound agency and democratic commitment among previously overlooked corners of civic life. ABOUT THE SPEAKER Frances Cayton is the Einstein Moos Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law (CDDRL). Her book project, "How Civic Consciousness Shapes Democratic Resilience," examines how, why, and under what conditions civil society encourages individuals to depolarize and resist democratic erosion. Combining extensive organizational and bureaucratic data, elite and mass surveys, experiments, and interview evidence, she demonstrates how informal and apolitical subsets of civic life retain critical latent democratic potential. More broadly, her research probes the drivers and consequences of democratic engagement, primarily in Eastern Europe while also drawing comparison with other eroding democracies globally. Her research is published or forthcoming in numerous outlets, including the American Journal of Political Science and Perspectives on Politics . Her work has been supported by the US Departments of State and Education, as well as the American Political Science Association. Cayton holds a PhD in Government from Cornell University. She earned her AM from Harvard University's Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies and a BA from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
title: Frances Cayton — Civic Consciousness and the Limits of Attacks on Civil Society

description: Many applications in computational geophysics require modeling seismic wave propagation across a set of closely related subsurface models. In such cases, it is often preferable to recompute wavefields locally, only in regions of change, rather than across the full model. Immersive boundary conditions make this possible: they capture the full interaction between two domains while requiring recomputation only within the domain that changes. The same methodology also enables immersing a physical experiment inside a virtual numerical simulation. At ETH Zurich's Centre for Immersive Wave Experimentation, we are building a laboratory to explore cloaking, holography, 3D time-reversal, and low-frequency acoustic experiments. I will present the underlying methodology, instrumentation advances, and milestone experiments toward this facility. Speaker-suggested readings: Theodor S. Becker et al. ,Broadband acoustic invisibility and illusions.Sci. Adv.7,eabi9627(2021).DOI:10.1126/sciadv.abi9627 van Manen, D.-J., & Robertsson, J. O. A. (2022). Immersive wave experimentation and The Matrix. Acoustics Today , 18 (4), 40–48. https://doi.org/10.1121/AT.2022.18.4.40

description: This event is sponsored by the Center for South Asia. About the event What happens when a democratic state―still in the process of formation―commits to banning a substance, especially one as controversial as alcohol? This book traces the origins and evolution of alcohol prohibition in India, drawing on extensive archival research and rich vernacular sources to explain its surprising resilience over time. Since its inception, prohibition has served both as an ideal and a tool of state power―a dual role that has worked to shape its shifting trajectories. Each phase of enforcement has served to reaffirm prohibition's founding logic, thereby further embedding it in the machinery of governance―even as it has constrained its future implementation. Foregrounding intersections with caste and gender, the book illuminates how diverse social responses have made prohibition a deeply contested―sobering―yet enduring project. While prohibition may be a thing of the past in the West, history helps to keep it alive in India. Darinee Alagirisamy's first monograph, Sober State: Origins of Alcohol Prohibition in India, was published by Cambridge University Press as part of the ICAS: MP book series, “Metamorphoses of the Political” in early 2026. The first book to be published on prohibition's origins in India, the book explains the reasons for the policy's persistence, despite its being a sobering site of consensus-building for successive governments. Sober State was supported by the NUS FASS Book Strategising Workshop Grant and FASS Book Publicity Scheme. About the author Alagirisamy is a historian of modern India and the Indian Ocean World, specialising in the political economy of social policy in the colonial and early postcolonial periods. Her fluency in Tamil, Telugu, and Hindi supports her multi-sited research. She earned her PhD in History and MPhil in Modern South Asian Studies (Distinction) from Cambridge University, where she held the Gates Cambridge Scholarship and Holland Rose Studentship. She received the CA Bayly Best Dissertation Prize for her MPhil Her peer-reviewed articles on the Dravidian movement's transnational impact, and the politics of alcohol prohibition in India have been published in Modern Asian Studies and The Indian Economic and Social History Review. She currently serves as Deputy Head of the South Asian Studies Programme at NUS. An experienced educator, she convenes large undergraduate lectures and smaller seminar-style classes, and supervise graduate students on various topics in modern Indian history.

description: The video game character creation screen represents the clearest aesthetic iteration of the medium’s promise of agency. The player is given the ability to create a self-insert character or a fantastical projection and then become whoever they want to be within the game world curated by the designer. Yet, the UI design of character creation screens undercuts that promise of agency by typically making the default created character align with the typical video game protagonist: white, male, muscular, and conventionally attractive. Combining both qualitative readings of select character creation screens with quantitative analysis of a larger corpus of character creators, this talk explores the default created character presented in over 200 video games from 1984 to 2026, spanning genres from the CRPG to the cozy sim to the sports game. In doing so, the talk asks if the standard default starting character creates and sustains a racial aesthetic, one in which the player is always implicitly a white guy. About the Speaker Austin Anderson PhD is a Provostial Fellow at Stanford University and Director of the Stanford Critical Game Studies Lab. He studies how games are enmeshed with race, gender, and class while also examining the liberatory potentials of gameworlds. His first book project, Racial Recursivity: A Methodology for Critical Race Game Studies , creates a formalist framework for analyzing the racial aesthetics of videogames. He has published in the fields of game studies, African American literary studies, and comic studies, and his work has appeared in the Journal of Gaming & Virtual Worlds, Transformative Works and Culture, Electronic Book Review, KULA, The Comparatist, Popular Culture Review, ADE Bulletin, ASAP/Review , and other outlets. He currently serves on the Multiplay Editorial Board and the SCMS Precarious Labor Committee. Lunch at 11:45 a.m. for in-person attendees Register to join online

This presentation, organized in collaboration with the Slavery and Freedom workshop, considers the centrality of enslaved people's lived experiences to the history of capitalism in the United States. description: We Care About What You Care About: Using Reason-Specific Interventions to Encourage Sustainable Choices Behavioral change is essential for climate change mitigation and adaptation. However, interventions encouraging sustainable choices often do not have the desired effect. To address this, we examined consumers' mental representations of environmentally consequential behaviors across seven situations to understand the reasons underlying sustainable and unsustainable choices. Using large language model-based topic modeling, we identified relevant reasons from open-ended responses underlying consumers' choices across seven situations. These reasons can be divided into situation-specific reasons, such as taste, which are mainly associated with a single situation, and general reasons, such as costs, which are applicable across situations. We applied these insights in two field experiments, in which participants received messages encouraging less meat and dairy consumption or reducing their shower duration. We randomly varied the message content, using situation-specific or general reasons. Only situation-specific messages significantly reduced meat and dairy consumption, while only general messages reduced shower duration during the 7-day study. We conclude that different situations are governed by different reasons and that interventions are most effective when they appeal to the reasons most central to the targeted behavior in that situation. Our results offer promising opportunities for developing more effective interventions by examining mental representations of the target behavior. Bio Antonia Krefeld-Schwalb, is associate professor of Marketing at RSM. She studies and teaches the impact of individual differences on responses to marketing and policy measures to improve targeting and segmentation. Her substantive focus is on sustainable consumer behaviour and adaptation to climate risk, and how to make persuasive messages such as emails and text messages as well as incentives more effective.
title: Environmental Behavioral Sciences Seminar with Antonia Krefeld-Schwalb

description: Extreme environments place stringent demands on materials used in building construction and thermal insulation for a wide range of industries. In Arctic communities, geographic remoteness leads to fragile supply chains, energy-intensive production and transportation, and unavoidable end-of-life impacts. Climate change further intensifies these demands. This seminar presents fungal biotechnology as an alternative to traditional building materials to address these challenges to human and planetary health. In particular, foamed mycelium biocomposite thermal insulation is presented as a scaled case study for direct integration into Alaskan homes. These materials have been developed as heavily insulating, robust, fire-resistant alternatives to traditional insulation. During this seminar, we will share applied projects that utilize these properties, including the “MyCell” wall system and the cold-chain “CoFoam” cooler for seafood and medicines shipping. Each of these deployments explore the integration of carbon storage, thermal regulation, and economic circularity. Particular attention is given to Arctic coastal communities, where microplastics pollution, traditional subsistence, thermal stress, and community vulnerability intersect. Additionally, we will discuss how genetic and process engineering can enable greater control over fungal growth properties including chitin production, hyphal morphology, microstructure, and cell-wall strength.
title: Invited Presentation, Building with Mushrooms at the Extremes: Design of Mycelium Biocomposite Construction Materials for Arctic Environments with Dr. Philippe Amstislavski

description: What can a whale, a dumpling, and an endangered clouded leopard tell us about belonging? Join artist and designer Yiying Lu, creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, for an opening talk celebrating Wild & Bright , an exhibition of nine large-scale digital paintings from her multi-year series on endangered species, on view in Hohbach Hall at Green Library through 2028. Lu will trace the unexpected creative path connecting these seemingly different worlds: from a personal illustration that became Twitter’s Fail Whale in 2008, to emoji designed to expand the world’s shared visual vocabulary, to a red panda created for a Bay Area AAPI night market that opened an entirely new direction in her practice. That exploration eventually led Lu to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, where her logo design for COP15 received an Award of Honor, and to support from the Adobe Creative Residency Community Fund. Wild & Bright began on August 4, 2020, International Clouded Leopard Day, with the clouded leopard as the first animal in the series. The work has since returned to the community in new ways. In 2025, sixteen pieces from the series were featured at a San Francisco Zoo fundraising gala, bringing art, storytelling, and wildlife conservation together. Across Lu’s work runs a central question: What does it take to make someone, or something, feel like it belongs in the picture? She approaches belonging as a design inquiry: whether the subject is a species losing its natural habitat, a culture missing from a global visual language, or a whale that made failure feel unexpectedly human. Following the presentation, Lu will join Professor Thomas S. Mullaney for a conversation about language, technology, and how visual systems decide who becomes visible. The program will conclude with an audience Q&A. The event takes place in the lead-up to World Animal Day on October 4. About Yiying Lu Yiying Lu is an award-winning artist, designer, and creative leader working at the intersection of art, technology, culture, and human experience. For nearly two decades, her practice has moved across digital culture, brand systems, public art, creative technology, and civic life, translating complex ideas into visual experiences that connect across cultures and communities. She is the creator of Twitter’s Fail Whale and has designed and successfully proposed six emoji adopted into the Unicode Standard, including the dumpling and boba tea. She previously served as Global Creative Director at 500 Global and as a San Francisco Arts Commissioner, appointed by the Mayor of San Francisco. She currently leads Happy Creative Land, a San Francisco-based innovation studio, and serves as an Adobe Global Creative Ambassador and a committee member of the UNESCO Chair in Digital Futures at Stanford. Her creative collaborations have included Disney, Apple, Google, Airbnb, Adobe, and NYU Shanghai. She has spoken at SXSW, Web Summit, TEDx, Today at Apple, and Talks at Google, and her work has been featured in The New York Times , BBC, TIME , The Atlantic , WIRED , and The Wall Street Journal . Lu has been recognized by Fast Company as one of its Most Creative People in Business, by Microsoft as a Top 10 Leader in Innovation, and by the Shorty Awards as its inaugural winner in Design. Born in Shanghai, educated in Sydney and London, and based in San Francisco, Lu brings a lived global perspective to the ways design and storytelling can create connections across cultures, communities, and generations. About Thomas Mullaney Thomas S. Mullaney is Professor of History and Professor of East Asian Languages and Cultures, by courtesy. He is also the Kluge Chair in Technology and Society at the Library of Congress, and a Guggenheim Fellow. He is the author or lead editor of 7 books, including The Chinese Typewriter (winner of the Fairbank prize), Your Computer is on Fire , Coming to Terms with the Nation: Ethnic Classification in Modern China , and the forthcoming The Chinese Computer—the first comprehensive history of Chinese-language computing. His writings have appeared in the Journal of Asian Studies, Technology & Culture, Aeon, Foreign Affairs, and Foreign Policy, and his work has been featured in the LA Times, The Atlantic, the BBC, and in invited lectures at Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and more. He holds a PhD from Columbia University.
title: Wild & Bright: Designing for Belonging | Artist Talk with Yiying Lu, in Conversation with Thomas S. Mullaney

description: Morad Tahbaz, in conversation with Abbas Milani. Morad Tahbaz’s new memoir, Green Parrots: A Memoir of Survival in Iran’s Evin Prison (Simon and Schuster, 2026), offers a rare window into contemporary Iran. While wrongfully imprisoned for nearly six years after being falsely accused of espionage while conducting wildlife conservation work, he experienced firsthand the realities of Evin Prison, the fragility of civil society, and the human cost of hostage diplomacy. Since his release in September 2023, he has become a thoughtful voice on Iran, wrongful detention, conservation, and the role of creativity in sustaining hope under extraordinary circumstances. While Green Parrots recounts Tahbaz’s years in prison, it is ultimately a story about resilience. Throughout his imprisonment, Tahbaz turned to art as a means of survival, creating drawings, sculptures, and he designed Persian carpets inspired by Iran's wildlife and artistic traditions. Today, one of his sculptures is part of the permanent collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, underscoring the enduring connection between his creative work and the country that shaped it. Morad Tahbaz is a conservationist, artist, and former political prisoner. In 2008, he co-founded the Persian Wildlife Heritage Foundation, which documented endangered species including Asiatic cheetahs and Persian leopards across Iran. In January 2018, he was arrested on fabricated espionage charges and spent sixty-eight months in Iran’s notorious Evin Prison, including four months in solitary confinement. A graduate of Colgate University (BA) and Columbia University (MBA), he spent his career supporting wildlife conservation across three continents before his imprisonment made him the subject of international hostage negotiations. He was released in September 2023 as part of a high-profile diplomatic agreement. Since his release, he has advocated for other wrongfully detained citizens and for continued attention to Iranian conservation. He lives in Connecticut with his wife Vida. description: Europe is commonly narrated from its historical centers. Political ideas, cultural innovation, and modernity itself are assumed to originate in places such as Paris, London, or Berlin before spreading to the continent's margins. Georgia usually appears in this narrative, if at all, as a distant periphery whose history merely reflects developments elsewhere. This lecture argues that such a view is historically misleading. Rather than treating Georgia as Europe's edge, it proposes to read it as one of the places from which Europe's history becomes newly intelligible. Revisiting the invention of "Eastern Europe," Georgia's democratic experiments of the early twentieth century, the multilingual urban culture and avant-garde of Tbilisi, and the shared but uneven legacy of 1989, the lecture examines how supposedly peripheral experiences challenge established narratives of European modernity. The aim is neither to "include" Georgia in an already existing European story nor simply to correct a geographical blind spot. Rather, the lecture argues that Europe's history itself changes once it is reconstructed from places long regarded as peripheral. Georgia thus emerges not as an exception but as a vantage point from which the cultural and political history of modern Europe can be reconsidered. RSVP here. Zaal Andronikashvili is Professor of Cultural Studies at Ilia State University in Tbilisi and a Research Fellow at the Leibniz Center for Literary and Cultural Research (ZfL) in Berlin. A literary scholar and cultural historian, he has spent much of his career situating Georgia within broader European and global histories while rethinking those histories from the vantage point of Georgia. His work explores empire, modernity, multilingualism, and the cultural legacies of the Soviet and post-Soviet worlds, with particular attention to the South Caucasus. Rather than treating the region as a footnote to a European story told elsewhere, he argues that Georgia offers a distinctive vantage point from which to challenge conventional narratives of center and periphery. He has published widely in German, English, and Georgian.
title: Europe from Its Margins: Georgia and the Making of Modern Europe

description: In Illiberal Law and Development , Susan H. Whiting advances institutional economic theory with original survey and fieldwork data, addressing two puzzles in Chinese political economy: how economic development has occurred despite insecure property rights and weak rule of law and how the Chinese state has maintained political control amid unrest. Whiting answers these questions by focusing on the role of illiberal law in reassigning property rights and redirecting grievances. The book reveals that, in the context of technological change, a legal system that facilitates reassignment of land rights to higher-value uses plays an important and under-theorized role in promoting economic development. This system simultaneously represses conflict and asserts legitimacy. Comparing China to post-Glorious Revolution England and contemporary India, Whiting presents a critical new argument that brings the Chinese case more directly into debates in comparative politics about the role of the state in specifying property rights and maintaining authoritarian rule. Speaker: Susan H. Whiting is Professor of Political Science at the University of Washington. She is the author of Illiberal Law and Development: Property Rights and Conflict over Land in China (2026) and Power and Wealth in Rural China: The Political Economy of Institutional Change (2001), both published by Cambridge University Press. Her research on property rights, state capacity, “rule of law,” economic development, and civil society in China has been published in journals such as Comparative Political Studies , Studies in Comparative International Development , China Quarterly, Journal of Asian Studies, and Voluntas , as well as in edited volumes such as Holding China Together and Trust and Governance , among others. She holds a Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of Michigan and a B.A. in East Asian Studies from Yale University. At the University of Washington, she also holds adjunct appointments in the School of Law and the Jackson School of International Studies.
title: Illiberal Law and Development: Property Rights and Conflict over Land in China

The session emphasizes foundational concepts, hands-on exploration, and concrete examples that lower the barrier to working with large-scale geospatial data. Google Earth Engine is a cloud-based geospatial processing platform that combines a multi-petabyte catalog of satellite imagery and geospatial datasets with planetary-scale analysis capabilities. It enables users to explore environmental change, map patterns, and compute statistics across large spatial and temporal extents—without the need to download or locally store massive datasets. This workshop is geared toward participants who want to understand how satellite imagery and related datasets are structured, accessed, and analyzed using Earth Engine. The session will be hands-on and will use the Earth Engine JavaScript Code Editor throughout. description: Latin America’s economic performance is often depicted as a long sequence of repeated failures, including its contribution to global financial crises as well as its slow growth and intractable inequalities. This talk will review the region's growth and development in the last quarter century, including the commodity boom, a surprising decline in economic inequality, responses to the financial and Covid-19 crises, and the emergence of left-leaning governments that opted for pragmatic and orthodox macro policies mixed with innovative antipoverty programs. description: In just half a century, Taiwan transformed from an agricultural colony into an economic power, spurred by efforts of the authoritarian Republic of China government in land reform, farmers associations, and improved crop varieties. Yet overlooked is how Taiwan brought these practices to the developing world. In the Global Vanguard elucidates the history and impact of the “Taiwan model” of agrarian development by incorporating how Taiwanese experts took the country’s agrarian success and exported it throughout rural communities across Africa and Southeast Asia. Driven by the global Cold War and challenges to the Republic of China’s legitimacy, Taiwanese agricultural technicians and scientists shared their practices, which they claimed were better suited for poor, tropical societies in the developing world. These development missions were portrayed in Taiwan as proof of the Republic of China’s modernity and were crucial to how the ruling government sought to hold onto its contested position in the international system and its rule by martial law at home. This talk will draw especially from Chapter 4, on Taiwan’s agrarian development missions to the Republic of Vietnam.
title: In the Global Vanguard: Agrarian Development and the Making of Modern Taiwan

description: Shagayeg Navabpour Postdoctoral Researcher, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford University Integrative Mental Health Laboratory (IMHL) [Duncan Lab] From Genetic Risk to Brain Cell Types: Insights from Psychiatric and Neurodegenerative disorders Bio Shagayeg Navabpour is a Knight Initiative Brain Resilience Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford’s Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute, where she works with Dr. Laramie Duncan in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences. She earned her BS in Biology and MS in Physiology from the University of Tehran, where she studied the endocannabinoid system in reward learning. After investigating genetic variation and brain structure in chimpanzees at Georgia State University, she completed her PhD in Translational Biology, Medicine, and Health at Virginia Tech with Dr. Timothy Jarome. Her doctoral research examined the molecular mechanisms of fear-memory formation, including epigenetic and chromatin dynamics and ubiquitin signaling. Now working at the intersection of human genomics and single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics, Dr. Navabpour maps genetic risk for psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders onto specific human brain cell types. Across her experimental and computational work, she is guided by a central question: Why are particular brain cells, and particular individuals, vulnerable to disease while others remain resilient? Shaghayegh has mentored undergraduate students at Stanford, Virginia Tech, and University of Tehran. She is also an actor and theater producer who explores the performing arts as a way to communicate neuroscience. Abstract Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified many regions of the genome associated with brain disorders, but these findings do not directly reveal where in the brain genetic risk acts. Recent single-nucleus transcriptomic atlases provide an opportunity to connect genetic associations to the molecular profiles of precisely defined human brain cell types. In this talk, Dr. Navabpour will describe an approach that integrates genome-wide association results with cell-type-specific gene expression across the human brain. Using psychiatric disorders as examples, she will show how this framework can move from broad genetic associations to specific neuronal populations and the brain regions in which they are found. She will then place these findings in the broader context of neurodegenerative disease. In Alzheimer’s disease, genetic risk points strongly toward microglia, highlighting the importance of non-neuronal immune mechanisms. In Parkinson’s disease, the strongest signals are concentrated among neuronal populations found primarily in the basal ganglia, as expected, but with newer brain atlases allowing these populations to be characterized at increasingly precise levels. Together, these examples demonstrate how mapping genetic risk to specific human brain cell types can provide a biologically meaningful bridge from genetic risk to disease mechanism and help prioritize cellular systems for further investigation and opens up new avenues for better targeted therapeutic strategies. Scott Dixon Prof. Scott Dixon, Department of Biology, Stanford University Dixon Lab Regulation of non-apoptotic cell death by disease-associated genes in the endolysosomal network Bio Scott is a Professor in the Department of Biology. As a postdoctoral fellow at Columbia University, he trained as a cell biologist and chemical biologist and helped discover the process of ferroptosis. His lab is currently focused on the regulation of non-apoptotic cell death in various disease contexts. Abstract The endolysosomal system is necessary for proper protein sorting and disposal. Mutations in various endolysosomal genes can contribute to neurological disease. We find that some of these genes, including CLN1 (PPT1) and DNAJC13, are important regulators of a novel form of non-apoptotic cell death termed lipid-dependent necrosis. I will present our latest insights into the nature of this unusual lethal mechanism and how disease-associated genes modulate cell death. Our results could help understand how these mutations contribute to cell death in the nervous system. About the Series The first Monday of each month, the Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience will host monthly seminars to bring together awardees, affiliated professors and students for a series of talks. Two speakers will discuss their brain resilience research, experiences in the field, and answer questions about their work. To support our researchers' participation, these seminars are not streamed/recorded and are only open to members of the Stanford community.
title: Shagayeg Navabpour  and Scott Dixon

description: Elizabeth Jun PhD Student, Nuyujukian Lab, Stanford University ( profile , lab website ) Elizabeth Jun is a neuroscience PhD Candidate at Stanford University and NIH F31 Predoctoral Fellow funded through National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS). Her research interests lie in understanding how large networks of neurons coordinate together to perform computations and support a wide range of behaviors in different contexts. Specifically in her thesis work, advised by Dr. Paul Nuyujukian in the Brain Interfacing Laboratory, she aims to understand how the brain can flexibly support a wide range of complex movements that are supported by a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. She is interested in connecting features of high-dimensional population data to similar behaviors in different contexts, and exploring in general how high-dimensional population features relate back to properties of the neural circuit. Investigating preserved neural motifs across and within tasks in premotor cortex Abstract Motor systems neuroscience studies how populations of motor cortical neurons coordinate to perform motor computations, but less is known about how large repertoires of movements are flexibly generated from a fixed set of fundamental motor computations. There is an emerging idea of conserved neural “modules”, or recurring neural activity patterns deploying computations through dynamics, that may serve as elementary building blocks for performing the same fundamental computation across a wide array of contexts. However, exactly what feature of neural dynamics is “recurring” and fundamentally conserved, if any, when performing the same motor computation within a wide range of reach sequence and kinematic contexts has yet to be shown and characterized empirically. To investigate this, we trained an animal implanted with a 96-channel Utah array in premotor cortex to perform 4 visually guided arm reaching motor tasks that are composed of unique combinations of 5 distinct motor processes (preparation, initiation, execution, hold, error correction) implemented in various reach conditions, where the same process can reappear across tasks and reappear again within tasks. This design allows us to test the hypothesis that premotor dynamics reuse conserved neural dynamics for performing the same motor computational process, but potentially implemented in different locations and orientations in population state space when reperformed across tasks, repeated in a sequence within tasks, and in different kinematic conditions. In this talk, I will explore systematically testing this hypothesis for all 5 motor processes to understand whether there are general organizing principles for premotor dynamics associated with deploying the same fundamental motor computation in a range of tasks, sequences, and kinematic contexts. description: Clinical Mind AI: Building an International AI Platform for Health Professions Education and the Learning Sciences HAI Seminar with Marcos Santiago Rojas Pino and Thomas Caruso Visit our website to learn more about the event agenda, speakers, and other details Clinical Mind AI is a Stanford-developed, international collaborative platform designed to strengthen clinical reasoning education through AI-simulated patient encounters across health professions. The platform enables educators to create clinical cases aligned with their local curricula, learning goals, languages, and assessment needs, while giving learners repeated opportunities to practice open-ended history-taking, diagnostic reasoning, and communication. The seminar will present the motivation for Clinical Mind AI, its design principles, and how the platform is being used by educators and institutions across countries to support scalable, instructor-centered clinical simulation. The talk will also discuss Clinical Mind AI as a research infrastructure for studying learning in clinical reasoning tasks. We will describe how learner interactions with AI-simulated patients can generate interpretable evidence about reasoning processes, including how students gather information, update hypotheses, document findings, and respond to feedback. The seminar will focus on broader questions at the intersection of AI, medical education, and learning science: how to build AI systems that preserve instructor agency, support multilingual and cross-institutional implementation, produce actionable insights for educators, and contribute to a more rigorous evidence base for AI-supported health professions education.

description: Session Description: For well over a century, filmmakers have been shooting documentaries in West and Central Africa, a region that included the colonies of French West and Equatorial Africa and now encompasses fourteen nations and nearly 200 million people. These films played a crucial role in the development of both European and African cinemas yet have been largely ignored by scholars. In the wake of fifty years of French colonial documentary in sub-Saharan Africa- propaganda-infused travel, hunting, expedition, and ethnographic films- African directors reclaimed their cinematic image by challenging outsider claims to authenticity and developing new models for nonfiction. I will highlight the nearly forgotten innovations of the decades following independence to demonstrate how, in a complex network of images and languages and across a dynamic range of modes, African documentarists remade a global art form rooted in oppression, exoticization, and a simplistic conception of filmic realism. Speaker Bio: Rachel Gabara is the Nancy Gillespie Brinning Professor in French at the University of Georgia, where her teaching focuses on nonfiction and historical fiction from Europe and sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to Documentary Objectives , published earlier this year by Indiana University Press, Gabara’s recent articles address early African film criticism ( Global Movie Magazine Networks , University of California Press), cinephilia and modernism in African cinema of the late 1960s and early 70s ( Modernism/modernity) , and contemporary debates about restitution and archives ( Contemporary French Civilization ). Her research in Burkina Faso, Senegal, and France has been supported by the Fulbright Scholar Program, the American Philosophical Society, and the National Endowment for the Humanities. https://iupress.org/9780253074805/documentary-objectives /

How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present. The exhibition traces a series of interconnected currents — ecological, infrastructural, technological, personal, creative, and political — that have shaped both artistic production and everyday life in Northern California. Arranged thematically across time and media, California Current places historical works in conversation with contemporary ones, emphasizing both continuity and change. Together, they ask: What has drawn so many people to this region? What has allowed communities and creative practices to take root here? description: How does the local presence of an authoritarian power shape citizens' commitment to democracy? Existing theories suggest engagement with authoritarian states should weaken democratic commitment through norm diffusion, accommodation, or authoritarian learning. This paper challenges that expectation by examining Chinese development finance in Latin America. Using geocoded data, it estimates the subnational effect of exposure to Chinese aid on democratic attitudes. Exposure increases support for democracy rather than undermining it. The effect is strongest in authoritarian and weakly democratic settings and absent in consolidated democracies. Exposure does not improve perceptions of China or the United States, casting doubt on soft power or foreign-comparison explanations. Instead, the paper argues that visible Chinese projects make incumbents' authoritarian character more salient, triggering an accountability response. These findings recast authoritarian external influence as a contingent catalyst for democratic reinforcement. ABOUT THE SPEAKER Marcela Ibáñez is a Visiting Postdoctoral Fellow at CDDRL and is a Postdoctoral Researcher at the Chair of Political Economy and Development at the University of Zurich. She holds a Ph.D. in Political Science from the University of Mannheim. Her work lies at the intersection of political economy, development, and vulnerability reduction. Her research interests include inequality in low and middle-income economies, sustainability and development programs, equality of opportunity, development and security after peace agreements, and party politics after civil war. Methodologically, she resorts to (quasi) experimental designs, survey designs, and quantitative text analysis.
title: Marcela Ibáñez — Authoritarian Aid and Democratic Attitudes: Backlash, Not Diffusion

description: Practical Geoengineering Carbon dioxide emissions seem set to peak this decade, but even if emissions were suddenly reduced to zero Earth will stay hot for thousands of years. Cooling Earth this century requires that emissions cuts be supplemented with either carbon removal or sunlight reflection, or both. I will focus on practical steps towards sunlight reflection using stratospheric sulfate aerosols that could enable a significant decrease in warming by mid-century. Bio David Keith has worked near the interface between climate science, energy technology, and public policy since 1990. He took first in Canada’s national physics prize exam, won MIT’s prize for excellence in experimental physics, and was one of TIME Magazine’s Heroes of the Environment. David is Professor of Geophysical Sciences and founding faculty director of the Climate Systems Engineering initiative at the University of Chicago. Best known for his work on the science, technology, and public policy of solar geoengineering, David led the development of Harvard’s Solar Geoengineering Research Program before moving to Chicago in 2023. His policy work has ranged from analysis of electricity markets and carbon prices to research on public and expert perceptions of risky technologies. David’s hardware work includes the first interferometer for atoms, a high-accuracy infrared spectrometer for NASA’s ER-2, the development of Carbon Engineering’s air contactor, and the development of a stratospheric propelled balloon experiment for solar geoengineering. David founded of Carbon Engineering , a Canadian company developing technology to capture CO2from ambient air. David teaches science and technology policy, climate science, and solar geoengineering. He has reached >150,000 students worldwide with an edX energy course. David is author of >200 academic publications with total citation count of >20,000. He has written for the public in op-eds and A Case for Climate Engineering . For more details, please visit David’s website here .

description: In the decades following World War II, American social scientists turned to the study of Japanese society as an emerging ally and fellow capitalist democracy. At a time when influential theories of modernization predicted the decline of kinship, community, hierarchy, and collective obligation, Japan presented a puzzle. It was an advanced industrial and capitalist society in which village, family, corporate welfare, and moral persuasion in public institutions played powerful roles in organizing everyday life. ​This talk examines how postwar scholars treated Japan not simply as an object of study but as a site for thinking through a larger problem in modern social thought: the relationship between individual freedom and social solidarity. Drawing on chapters from a larger book project, I revisit three influential studies of Japan: Ruth Benedict's The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946), Ezra Vogel's Japan's New Middle Class (1963), and Thomas Rohlen's For Harmony and Strength (1974). I argue that these works are best understood not only as interpretations of Japan but also as reflections on what I call the "social question" in postwar thought: how modern societies cultivate attachment, obligation, welfare, and collective purpose while preserving democratic freedoms and individual autonomy. By placing these texts in conversation, the talk suggests that postwar Japan functioned as a distinctive archive for thinking about enduring questions of social reproduction and social solidarity in democratic life. This event is open to the public. Please RSVP here . ​ About the speaker: ​Amy Borovoy is a cultural anthropologist and professor in the Department of East Asian Studies at Princeton University. She is interested in the ways in which societies provide social care to their citizens and the costs of this care. Her book, The Too-Good Wife (2005), explored heavy drinking in Japan and its effects on the wives who must cope with their husbands’ alcoholism. She has also written on social withdrawal, public health and mass screening, and Covid-19 containment in Japan. Her manuscript in progress, In Search of Social Solidarity, explores how American social scientists after World War II made sense of postwar Japan not simply as an object of study but as a site for thinking through a larger problem in modern social thought: the relationship between individual autonomy and social solidarity, community welfare, and the socialization of the self.
title: The Fate of the Social in Modern Life: American Social Scientists and Japan as Archive

description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The Bowes Art and Architecture Library exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. This Study Evening brings together Geraldine Johnson and Alexander Nemerov to discuss the role of the detail in art history, moderated by the exhibition’s curator, Altair Brandon-Salmon. Geraldine Johnson is Associate Professor in the History of Art at the University of Oxford. She will discuss the Italian sculptor-photographer Medardo Rosso (1858-1928) and his deployment of details from installation shots taken at the 1904 Salon d'Automne in Paris in his own photographs and collages. He used these details to produce new works of aesthetic interest in their own right, as well as in a campaign waged through the art press to prove that he was the true inventor of 'Impressionist' sculpture. By cropping photographs of work by Modern 'masters' such as Rodin and Cézanne, whom he saw as rivals, and Old masters such as Michelangelo, Rosso created an entirely new form of photographic assemblage that undermined established notions of sculptural materiality and conventions for photographing sculpture. The result was, as Rosalind Krauss suggests, a form of art-making that "gesture[s] toward the unseeable side of objects." Alexander Nemerov is the Carl and Marilynn Thoma Provostial Professor in the Arts and Humanities in the Department of Art and Art History at Stanford University. In his talk, he will focus on the book The Voices of Silence (1951), where André Malraux reproduces a detail from Rembrandt’s The Night Watch (1642), bestowing extraordinary importance on a figure who might otherwise seem sheerly of background interest. The detail, bringing out the strangeness, even eeriness of the figure—in effect, creating that strangeness (for the black-and-white detail is even odder than the figure in the painting)—Malraux creates a time-bound human: a figure bonded to Rembrandt’s time, and to the mid-20th century, and to some other time, not known to human beings, whose coordinates are outer space. Altair Brandon-Salmon is an art historian and a lecturer in the Civic, Liberal, and Global Education (COLLEGE) programme at Stanford University. He is a guest curator for Projects Twenty Two. description: The 2019 assassination of Paweł Adamowicz, Mayor of Gdańsk, marked a decisive moment in Poland’s political trajectory, revealing how anti immigrant rhetoric can harden into physical violence. This talk examines Adamowicz’s death as the culmination of a sustained campaign against pro integration politics – a campaign directed at him precisely because he advanced a vision of national belonging rooted in civic openness rather than ethnonationalism. Adamowicz’s integration agenda drew on Christian social teaching, including papal messages on migration and the Catholic principles embedded in Gdańsk’s Immigrant Integration Model. His approach aligned with Benjamin Barber’s conviction that cities, rather than nation states, function as democratic bulwarks: pragmatic, diverse, and dependent on newcomers for social and economic vitality. For Barber, immigrants do not threaten urban cohesion; they generate it, bringing skills, energy, and civic potential that strengthen cities’ capacity to innovate and govern. Adamowicz’s Christian inflected urban pluralism — grounded in hospitality, dignity, and shared responsibility — thus stood in stark contrast to Poland’s rising illiberal currents. This pluralism extended beyond migration. Adamowicz championed LGBTQ+ inclusion through initiatives such as the Model for Equal Treatment, municipal anti discrimination programs, and public support for Gdańsk’s Equality March. These policies articulated a broader ethics of belonging: a city that protects its minorities protects its democratic future. Figures such as Karol Nawrocki (today serving as President of Poland) publicly attacked him, claiming that he was “a politician who does not recognize what is sacred,” a charge that inverted Adamowicz’s own reliance on Catholic doctrine to defend inclusion. Yet the aftermath of the assassination revealed a different trajectory than the one intended by his attackers. Instead of producing civic chaos or deepening polarization, Adamowicz’s death generated an unprecedented public outpouring of grief and solidarity. In Gdańsk, tens of thousands mobilized around the very principles he had championed — openness, equality, and the protection of newcomers — reaffirming inclusion as the city’s guiding civic ethos. In the years since, Gdańsk has continued to develop policies rooted in this ethic, demonstrating how urban governance can transform trauma into a renewed commitment to democratic pluralism. This talk argues that Adamowicz’s legacy lies not only in the threats he faced, but in the inclusive civic imagination that survived him: a model of urban democracy in which cities respond to violence not with fear, but with deeper solidarity and an expanded sense of who belongs. Please RSVP here. Izabela Morska is a Polish scholar and writer, Professor of English and American Studies at the University of Gdańsk. Her current research on Paweł Adamowicz examines civic ethics, pluralism, and the cultural imaginaries of democracy. She holds an MA from the University of Gdańsk, a PhD from the Polish Academy of Sciences, and an MFA from Mills College, and has held research appointments at the University College Dublin Humanities Institute, the Open Society Archives at CEU Budapest, the Russian Institute for Advanced Study in Moscow, and the Beatrice Bain Research Group at UC Berkeley. A recipient of the Polish Ministry of Culture scholarship for The Legacy of Paweł Adamowicz project, she works at the intersection of media studies, border studies, and narrative ethics. Her teaching and writing explore American political imaginaries, embodiment narratives, subaltern studies, and creative nonfiction.
title: Paweł Adamowicz and the Civic Ethos of Inclusion: Urban Democracy After the Assassination

description: Join us for the 16th Bita Prize for Persian Arts celebrating acclaimed Iranian musician Sima Bina. Sima Bina is a renowned Iranian folk singer, songwriter, and researcher. She is celebrated for her contributions to preserving and promoting Persian folk music and culture. Sima Bina was born in 1945, in Khorasan, Iran. Her passion for folk music emerged from her childhood experiences, as she grew up surrounded by traditional Persian melodies and rhythms. She began singing at an early age and was particularly drawn to the rich tapestry of regional folk songs from different parts of Iran. Her professional career grew in the 1960s when she started performing publicly and recording albums. Bina's distinctive voice and her ability to interpret traditional songs with authenticity quickly earned her recognition within Iran and abroad. Bina is also a dedicated researcher and educator. Throughout her career, Bina has tirelessly worked to collect, document, and preserve Persian folk music, traveling to remote regions of Iran to learn from local musicians and record their songs. She has amassed an extensive repertoire of folk songs representing various ethnic groups and regions of Iran, from Kurdish lullabies to Baluchi melodies. She has published books on Persian folk music and has lectured at universities and cultural institutions around the world, sharing her knowledge and passion for Iranian musical heritage. Bina's impact on Persian folk music extends beyond her own performances. She has mentored and inspired numerous musicians, both in Iran and internationally, and her work continues to influence the revival and appreciation of traditional Iranian music. Despite the restrictions imposed on women's voices by the Islamic Republic of Iran, particularly during the 1980s and 1990s, Bina showed remarkable resilience and determination in preserving Iran's musical heritage. During this period, when cultural activities were heavily regulated, Bina took significant risks by organizing music workshops and clandestinely teaching Iranian women traditional music. These underground efforts played a crucial role in ensuring the transmission of Persian folk music to future generations and empowering women to express themselves through music, despite societal constraints. Despite facing challenges and restrictions in her homeland, Bina has remained steadfast in her commitment to preserving and promoting Persian folk music. Her contributions to Iranian cultural heritage have earned her numerous accolades and awards, solidifying her legacy as one of Iran's most beloved folk singers and cultural ambassadors.

description: Session Description The second Trump administration has undertaken a series of decisions with profound and lasting consequences for the health and survival of Africa’s children. The abrupt dismantling of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) is projected to result in approximately 14 million excess deaths, the majority concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa. Concurrently, the decision to initiate hostilities with Iran and the ensuing disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have severely constrained global fertilizer exports to African markets. Modeling informed by NASA agricultural forecasts indicates that the 2027 growing season in the Sahel is at high risk of significant production shortfalls and elevated famine risk. This talk presents ongoing research from the Stanford Geopolitical Human Impact Research Lab on the cascading effects of geopolitical decisions on human health. It focuses specifically on the projected impacts of the Strait of Hormuz crisis on food security and child nutrition across the Sahel in the 2027 season and outlines concrete policy options through which the United States can still act to avert a larger-scale humanitarian catastrophe. Speaker Bio Dr. Ruth Gibson is the Founding Executive Director of the Stanford Geopolitical Human Impact Research Lab, the first research lab at Stanford University dedicated to examining how geopolitical decisions shape human lives, with particular attention to children. Based in the Department of Pediatrics at the School of Medicine, the Research Lab brings together health modeling, open-source intelligence, and international humanitarian law to produce rigorous, policy-relevant scholarship. She co-leads The Lancet Series on Foreign Engagement and Health in an Era of Geopolitical Crisis with Professor Gary Darmstadt. Dr. Gibson earned her PhD in geopolitical coercion and global health from the University of British Columbia and completed postdoctoral training at Stanford’s Center for International Security and Cooperation from 2022 to 2025. Drawing on more than a decade of international global health experience across five continents, her research focuses on the health consequences of sanctions, blockades, and armed conflict, especially their effects on maternal and child health.
title: The Future of Health in Africa: How U.S. Presidential Decisions Are Shaping a Generation of African Children - Dr. Ruth Gibson

Taylor is Professor of Comparative Media Studies at MITand affiliate faculty member in Anthropology and Women’s and Gender Studies.
