description: Citizenship is conventionally understood as a source of rights and protection. It is also a source of dependency: states retain distinctive authority over passports, legal identities, civil status, and mobility that citizens need even when they live abroad. Under authoritarianism, these dependencies become instruments of political control. The study introduces extraterritorial authoritarian citizenship, a continuing relationship in which emigrants depend on origin-state institutions whose provision of nominally universal rights is politically conditional. It generates latent leverage: the capacity to impose costs without exercising it against anyone in particular. Emigrants may curb dissent even when never targeted, and transnational repression activates leverage already at work. Using a four-wave panel survey of 4,000+ Russian emigrants in over 100 countries and 500+ interviews, the authors show that what emigrants fear is the open-ended legal and administrative reach of the origin state rather than targeted violence, that this fear suppresses contentious activism specifically, and that only the protection of another state reduces it. (In collaboration with Emil Kamalov and Karolina Nugumanova). ABOUT THE SPEAKER Ivetta Sergeeva specializes in comparative social science, focusing on political behavior, civil society, citizenship and migration. In her research, she employs a mixed-methods approach, emphasizing surveys, statistical modeling, experiments, and interviews. Apart from her research skills, she has eight years of experience supervising projects in civil society and human rights organizations within the challenging context of contemporary Russia.
title: Ivetta Sergeeva — The Authoritarian Passport: How States Discipline Emigrants Without Repressing Them

description: Who decides what time it is? In Habsburg Bohemia, that question drew in nearly every other: nation and empire, identity and sovereignty, capital and a newly connected world. Railways and telegraphs created a time shared across distance, and with it a debate over who had the power to set it. Histories of time standardization have told a story of unification; histories of Habsburg sovereignty, meanwhile, have located its conflicts in diets and parliaments. This talk brings them together, asking how an empire tried to synchronize every local clock, where authority over time was located, and why time became a question of sovereignty. After 1867, Bohemia's unresolved constitutional status moved into the infrastructure of daily life: whose observatory produced noon, which meridian ran the trains, whose clocks kept the time. At stake was not only who ruled Bohemia, but how time could be controlled at all. By the turn of the century, Bohemians called their divided time dualismus, the word for the constitutional settlement itself. This talk traces these jurisdictional disputes over four decades from railway decrees to universal time. The lines of conflict did not run simply between empire and nation: German liberals, Czech nationalists, intellectuals, and businessmen appealed to historic rights, national identity, commercial interest, and civic embarrassment. Jurisdiction over time was scalar, dispersed across ministries, railway companies, international conferences, and municipal councils, and exercised through everyday practice; sovereignty over time was claimed everywhere but located nowhere. The talk closes by asking, as the satirists of the day did, whether any authority could make a polity agree on something as basic as noon. Jana Hunter is Assistant Professor at Stanford University, where she works on modern Central and Eastern Europe with particular interests in time, science and technology, modernity, and environmental change. Her first book project, Kingdom of Hours: The Transformation of Time in Habsburg Bohemia, 1848-1918, uses time as a lens to rethink the making of modern Central Europe. Rather than treating modern time as a single, accelerating rhythm, the study examines the coexistence of natural and industrial, religious and secular, nationalist and imperial, and mechanical and subjective temporalities that structured everyday life in late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Bohemia. Moving from rural villages and mining towns to Prague’s municipal councils and the Reichsrat, the book reconstructs how local actors reworked temporal regimes to serve imperial, national, regional, and commercial aims, offering a new framework for understanding modernization beyond the categories of nation and empire. Her second project, Testing Grounds: From Marx to Oppenheimer—Czechoslovakia’s Global Legacy, 1918-Present, traces how twentieth-century ideologies of modernity were lived, imposed, and resisted through the uranium-mining town of Jáchymov. Once dubbed the “cradle of the atomic bomb,” Jáchymov became a testing ground for successive empires and energy regimes, its landscape transformed by extractive ambition, political violence, and environmental fallout. Bringing Karl Marx’s ecological critique into dialogue with J. Robert Oppenheimer’s nuclear physics, the project reframes the history of militarized landscapes and energy transitions, situating East-Central Europe within global histories of extraction and environmental change. Hunter received her D.Phil. from the University of Oxford in 2024 and her M.Phil. from the University of Cambridge. She has held fellowships at Princeton University, the Czech Academy of Sciences, the University of Vienna, and the Herder Institute. Before joining Stanford, she was a Lecturer in Modern European History at New College, Oxford.

Navigating turbulent CNS waters Abstract The central nervous system was long viewed as an immune-privileged organ, largely isolated from peripheral physiology. Over the past decade, this paradigm has shifted. Our work has revealed that the brain continuously exchanges signals, cells, and molecules with the immune and lymphatic systems, and that these interactions are essential for normal brain function, aging, and disease. In this lecture, I will discuss recent discoveries that redefine the anatomical and physiological pathways connecting the brain to the rest of the body, including meningeal lymphatics, skull and vertebral bone marrow, and cerebrospinal fluid dynamics. I will also present emerging evidence that dysfunction of these systems contributes to neurological disorders and cognitive decline, highlighting new therapeutic opportunities at the interface of neuroscience and immunology. Jonathan Kipnis, PhD Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Immunology, Washington University at St. Louis Dr. Jonathan (Jony) Kipnis is BJC Investigator, Alan A. and Edith L. Wolff Distinguished Professor of Pathology and Immunology and Professor of Neurology, Neuroscience, and Neurosurgery at Washington University in St. Louis, School of Medicine. He is also the inaugural Director of Brain immunology and Glia (BIG) Center at Washington University. Jony graduated from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, where he was Sir Charles Clore Scholar and a recipient of distinguished prize for scientific achievements awarded by the Israeli Parliament, The Knesset. The Kipnis laboratory investigates the interactions between the immune system and the central nervous system, with a focus on the cellular and molecular mechanisms that govern brain function in health, aging, and neurological disease. His group demonstrated that normal brain function depends, in part, on an intact immune system and identified several cytokines as important neuromodulators. Most notably, his laboratory discovered the meningeal lymphatic vessels that drain the central nervous system into peripheral lymph nodes, revealing a direct anatomical link between the brain and the immune system. This finding reshaped the concept of central nervous system immune privilege and opened new avenues for studying neuroimmune interactions in health and disease, with implications for disorders including Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis, autism, and age-related cognitive decline. description: Join Maggie Dethloff, Assistant Curator of Photography and New Media, on this special tour of California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area . RSVP here . How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present. The exhibition traces a series of interconnected currents — ecological, infrastructural, technological, personal, creative, and political — that have shaped both artistic production and everyday life in Northern California. Arranged thematically across time and media, California Current places historical works in conversation with contemporary ones, emphasizing both continuity and change. Together, they ask: What has drawn so many people to this region? What has allowed communities and creative practices to take root here? And what continues to keep so many of us — despite the Bay Area’s contradictions, pressures, and constant reinvention — deeply connected to this place? Presented as part of the Further Triennial, this exhibition features works by artists Pacita Abad, Saif Azzuz (Libyan-Yurok), Robert Bechtle, Bernice Bing, Kota Ezawa, L. description: Bio: Matto Mildenberger is Assistant Professor of Political Science at UC Santa Barbara. His research explores the political drivers of policy inaction in the face of serious social and economic threats posed by global climate change. Straddling comparative political economy and political behavior, Mildenberger's work focusses on comparative climate policymaking and the dynamics of US climate opinion. His current book project compares the politics of carbon pricing across advanced economies, with a focus on the history of climate reforms in Australia, Norway and the United States. Other ongoing work explores public environmental behaviors, political ideology, and the relationship between economic and environmental policy preferences. A previous book, Dependent America? How Mexico and Canada Construct US Power (Toronto 2011, with Stephen Clarkson), explored the political economy of North American trade and security relationships.

description: About the event: China is practicing gray-zone coercion in the Indo-Pacific, deploying military vessels for drills in the waters between Taiwan and the Philippines. This “salami-slicing” strategy, advanced under Xi Jinping, incrementally escalates pressure on neighboring states while remaining below the threshold of open conflict. Disruption of critical sea lanes—through which fuel and food supplies transit—would have catastrophic implications for human populations dependent on uninterrupted maritime traffic. This talk presents research from the Stanford Geopolitical Coercion and Global Health Impact Initiative on maritime disruptions in the Indo-Pacific and what they would mean for human populations if maritime traffic were interrupted in a manner comparable to a closure of the Strait of Hormuz, with particular attention to effects on food security, energy access, and maternal and child health. About the speaker: Dr. Ruth Gibson is a Visiting Scholar at the Center for Innovation in Global Health, Affiliated Scholar at CISAC and the Founding Executive Director of the Stanford Geopolitical Human Impact Research Lab—the first research initiative at Stanford University dedicated to examining how geopolitical decisions shape human lives, with particular attention to children. Based in the Department of Pediatrics at the Stanford School of Medicine, the Initiative brings together health modeling, open-source intelligence, and international humanitarian law to produce rigorous, policy-relevant scholarship. She co-leads The Lancet Series on Foreign Engagement and Health in an Era of Geopolitical Crisis with Professor Gary Darmstadt. Dr. Gibson earned her PhD in geopolitical coercion and global health from the University of British Columbia and completed postdoctoral training at Stanford’s Center for International Security and Cooperation from 2022 to 2025. Drawing on more than a decade of international global health experience across five continents, her research focuses on the health consequences of sanctions, blockades, and armed conflict, especially their effects on maternal and child health.
title: When a “Salami Slice” Becomes a Maritime Blockade: China’s Maritime Disruptions in the Indo-Pacific and Consequences for Human Populations

description: Recent years have seen a push to recognize the east Roman state and its people for what and who they said they were — Romans — and not to hide that reality under the invented term “Byzantium,” which has always encoded negative stereotypes. In this talk, professor Kaldellis will discuss the ideologies and structural interests that have resisted acknowledging a Roman people in the east, ranging from western Eurocentrism to modern Greek nationalism. “Rome" has long been a foundational matrix for thinking about western identities and states: what would it look like if it made room to accommodate its eastern branch on an equal basis? RSVP here. Anthony Kaldellis is a professor of Classics at the University of Chicago. He has published widely on the history, culture, and literature of Byzantium, ranging from the fourth to the fifteenth centuries. His works include a new, comprehensive history of the eastern Roman empire: The New Roman Empire: A History of Byzantium (Oxford, 2023). Most recently he has published a new history of the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and a study of western perceptions of Byzantium from late antiquity to World War II (Phantom Byzantium). He has translated medieval Greek authors, including historians such as Prokopios, Attaleiates, and Laonikos Chalkokondyles, and is the host of the academic podcast “Byzantium & Friends,” going strong since 2019.
title: Who’s Afraid of the East Romans?

description: Catherine Murphy's new documentary, Reading the World , explores the work that Paulo Freire was doing in the years before writing "Pedagogy of the Oppressed" and "Education as the Practice of Freedom.” Especially focusing on the rural Northeastern town of Angicos, the film centers the voices of the few living students, and locates events in the historical context of 1960s. Catherine Murphy is a US..-based documentary filmmaker who has spent much of her career living and working in Latin America. She is the founder and director of Maestra Productions, a collaborative production house working at the intersection of arts, education, and social movements. Murphy has directed six films, including MAESTRA, about the a group of young women literacy teachers. Narrated by Pulitzer Prize–winning author Alice Walker, the film is distributed by Women Make Movies and has been translated into six languages. Leading Uruguayan author Eduardo Galeano drew on Murphy’s interviews for four short stories in his penultimate book, Espejos. Before turning to filmmaking, Murphy was a professor at NYU’s Center for Global Affairs. Her most recent film, about the early work of Brazilian educator Paulo Freire, was co-directed with Iris de Oliveira and premiered at the prestigious Gramado Film Festival in Brazil, where it won the Best Feature Documentary Award.

description: Jian Xiong Knight Initiative Brain Resilience Postdoctoral Scholar, Stanford University Abu-Remaileh Lab Regulation of Bis(Monoacylglycero)Phosphate in Neurodegeneration Bio & Abstract coming soon Fei Deng Postdoc, Stanford University Owen Lab Dynamic cholinergic modulation of cognitive function in Parkinson’s disease Bio Fei Deng is a postdoc in Scott Owen’s lab in the Neurosurgery Department. He is interested in neuromodulation and its applications to neurological diseases. He earned his Ph.D. from Peking University in 2023, where he developed genetically encoded serotonin sensors under the supervision of Professor Yulong Li. With a strong background in monitoring neuromodulators using advanced sensors and imaging techniques, he is dedicated to uncovering how neuromodulators shape complex brain functions and behaviors, currently focusing on the dynamics of acetylcholine signaling in the striatum during flexible learning and restorative interventions targeting the brain’s cholinergic system in Parkinson’s disease. Abstract The ability to adapt behavior in changing environments declines with normal aging and is further impaired in patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD). Dysregulated dopamine (DA) and acetylcholine (ACh) signaling in the striatum is thought to underline this deficit in flexible learning and represents an important therapeutic target. To uncover dynamics and functions of DA and ACh during flexible learning, I combined a two-spout licking task with dual-color fiber photometry recordings in healthy mice and a 6-OHDA model of PD. In healthy mice, unrewarded licking evoked a prominent rebound in ACh signaling. Strikingly, this ACh rebound was absent in the PD model, suggesting that it may play an important role in flexible learning. Indeed, pharmacological blockade of cholinergic signaling reduced both task engagement and switching ability, primarily through M4-type acetylcholine receptors. Dopamine depletion in the 6-OHDA PD model similarly impaired task performance, by reducing engagement and diminishing switching ability. Together, these findings identify dynamic cholinergic signaling as a key contributor to behavioral flexibility and suggest that restoring ACh modulation or its downstream signaling pathways may offer a strategy to alleviate PD-related cognitive decline while minimizing side effects. About the Series The first Monday of each month, the Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience will host monthly seminars to bring together awardees, affiliated professors and students for a series of talks. Two speakers will discuss their brain resilience research, experiences in the field, and answer questions about their work. To support our researchers' participation, these seminars are not streamed/recorded and are only open to members of the Stanford community.
title: Jian Xiong and Fei Deng

description: Abstract: When medical imaging mapped the neural deterioration of the legendary Hong Kong ink painter Irene Chou (1924-2011), she looked at her own brain X-rays and experienced a startling revelation: “I saw vital images of tree branches… that is life—my life.” In this lecture, Eugene Wang (Harvard University) reconsiders Chou’s art through the converging lenses of plant sensience, systems biology, and Buddhist-cum-Daoist meditative practice, revealing her paintings not as abstract landscapes but as experiments in biocosmic imagination. From the refuge of her father’s photographic darkroom in Shanghai to her solitary, obsessive sketches of “ten thousand trees” in Hong Kong’s dense woods, Chou turned ink into a means of self-preservation: thousands of rhythmic parallel lines became protective membranes, holding an endangered inner world against chaos. Bringing Charles Darwin’s studies of plant movement, Herbert Read’s modernist aesthetics, medical imaging, and the alchemical cosmology of breathing exercise into dialogue, Wang shows how Chou transformed illness and vulnerability into paintings of biocosmic imaginative reach—works that move from capillary and cell to vortex and galaxy, forging a radiant visual lexicon of resilience, renewal, and cosmic liberation. Bio: Eugene Y. Wang is the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Professor of Asian Art at Harvard University. A Guggenheim Fellow and art-history editor of the Encyclopedia of Buddhism , he is the author of Shaping the Lotus Sutra: Buddhist Visual Culture in Medieval China , recipient of Japan’s Sakamoto Nichijin Academic Achievement Award. Focused on the cognitive study of art, Wang’s research explores how images add up to function as worldmaking systems, and how art extends into biocosmic and psychocosmic dimensions. His work ranges from Asian Buddhist art and Chinese art history to immersive environments and digital media. He is the founding director of Harvard CAMLab, dedicated to the cognitive modeling of cultural systems. In 2024, Wang curated Mawangdui: Art of Life , an immersive exhibition designed and produced by CAMLab that attracted more than one million visitors and received the 2025 iF Design Award in Germany. CAMLab’s Digital Gandhara was named a 2026 AWHEIC Star of Outstanding by a global heritage-education initiative of WHITRAP, a UNESCO Category 2 Centre. Wang is currently leading a new CAMLab project, Digital Borobudur .
title: Eugene Wang: "Biocosmic Art; or How to Capture a Painter’s Brain?"

description: Abstract: This talk reexamines Borobudur through the transmission of Esoteric Buddhist teachings associated with Indian Tantric Buddhist master Vajrabodhi (671–741). It argues that Vajrabodhi’s activities in Java and China, his transmission of Tantric teachings to Amoghavajra, and the subsequent initiation of the Javanese monk Bianhong into the Garbhadhātu Maṇḍala by Amoghavajra’s disciple Huiguo created the historical and doctrinal framework for Borobudur’s construction. A three-dimensional Buddhist maṇḍala known as the shi 式 or “secret disc”, described in a Tang Buddhist text attributed to Vajrabodhi, closely parallels Borobudur’s architectural form, cosmological model, iconographic program of the Five Jina Buddhas, and solar symbolism. It proposes that Borobudur was conceived as a monumental celestial maṇḍala of Mahāvairocana, shaped by Vajrabodhi’s Esoteric Buddhist lineage and its cosmological vision. Vajrabodhi’s shi , however, was rooted in the traditional Chinese shi , whose origins can be traced to the Neolithic Liangzhu Culture of southeastern China. Bio: Anning Jing received his MA in Art History from Ohio State University in 1989 and PhD in Art History from Princeton University in 1993. He has been teaching Asian art at Michigan State University since 1995. His main publications include The Water God's Temple of the Guangsheng Monastery: Cosmic Function of Art, Ritual, and Theater (Leiden: Brill, 2002), Yuandai biha “Shenxianfuhui tu” ( The Yuan Murals “Assembly of the Immortals” ; Beijing: Beijing University Press, 2002, second edition 2016), Daojiao Quanzhenpai de gongguan, zaoxiang yu zushi (Temples, images and patriarchs of the Complete Realization School of Daoism; Beijing: Zhonghua shuju, 2012).
title: Anning Jing: "Borobudur and a Tantric Buddhist Maṇḍala Associated with Vajrabodhi (671–741)"

description: Join Joanna García Cherán, the Phyllis Wattis Assistant Curator of Native American Art, on this special tour of California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area . RSVP here . How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present. The exhibition traces a series of interconnected currents — ecological, infrastructural, technological, personal, creative, and political — that have shaped both artistic production and everyday life in Northern California. Arranged thematically across time and media, California Current places historical works in conversation with contemporary ones, emphasizing both continuity and change. Together, they ask: What has drawn so many people to this region? What has allowed communities and creative practices to take root here? And what continues to keep so many of us — despite the Bay Area’s contradictions, pressures, and constant reinvention — deeply connected to this place? Presented as part of the Further Triennial, this exhibition features works by artists Pacita Abad, Saif Azzuz (Libyan-Yurok), Robert Bechtle, Bernice Bing, Kota Ezawa, L. description: What can ancient work practices offer Silicon Valley today? Hidden in more than a thousand years of Sōtō Zen monastic codes, we can trace the development of what we might now call a 90-day serious role-playing game. Its purpose: to spiritually mature practitioners, separately and together, for their own benefit and that of all beings. In this lecture, we will explore aspects of Chinese, Japanese, and Western monastic work codes to find out how they promote human-hearted qualities such as generosity, morality, forbearance, and energy. Familiarity with these practices can help us illuminate the meaning and function of our responsibilities to ourselves, our work groups, our communities, and our world. 4:00pm - Guided Meditation (Room TBD) 7:00pm - Lecture (East Asia Library, Room 224) Bio: Shosan Victoria Austin began practicing Zen in 1971. She trained in the U.S., in India, and in Japan, and is entrusted as a Dharma heir in the lineage of Shunryu Suzuki Roshi (1999), an international Soto Zen priest (2005), and a Dharma teacher at San Francisco Zen Center (1999). Some of her previous San Francisco Zen Center roles include Work Leader, Tenzo, Tanto, and President. In 2022, she co-led the training and participation of the Ryoban (ceremonial assembly) for the Zenshuji 100th Anniversary Jukai-e in Los Angeles, a five-day retreat in which over 100 people received precept teachings and vows. In addition to her deep study and daily teaching of yogic aspects of meditation—in diverse settings including workplaces, institutions, and homes—Shosan serves as an Iyengar yoga teacher (1988), teacher educator (2003), assessor of new yoga teachers (2005), and Right Use of Power facilitator (2019). In her offerings, she emphasizes inclusion, accessibility, trauma sensitivity, and appropriate challenge, grounded in awareness of the possibility and presence of liberation.

description: The Creative Writing Program is pleased to announce the next event with the Mohr Visiting Poet: A Reading with Robin Coste Lewis . This event is open to Stanford affiliates and the general public. Registration is encouraged but not required; RSVP form to follow. ____ Robin Coste Lewis is a writer and artist. Lewis won the National Book Award for Voyage of the Sable Venus, her first collection of poetry. The book was also a finalist for the Hurston/Wright Legacy Award and the Los Angeles Times Book Award, and it was named one of the best books of the year by The New Yorker and The New York Times. Literary Hub named it one of the best books of the last twenty years. Lewis was the first African-American to ever win the National Book Award in a debut, and the first woman to do so since 1974. Her second book, To the Realization of Perfect Helplessness , was the winner of the PEN/Voelcker Award for Poetry and the NAACP Image Award for Outstanding Literary Work in Poetry. She is also the coauthor, with Kevin Young, of Robert Rauschenberg: Thirty-Four Illustrations for Dante’s Inferno, published by the Museum of Modern Art. Her latest book, Archive of Desire , was named by the Brooklyn Public Library as one of the best poetry collections of the year. The former poet laureate of Los Angeles, Lewis holds a PhD in poetry and visual studies from the University of Southern California, an MFA in poetry from New York University, an MTS in Sanskrit and comparative religious literature from the Divinity School at Harvard University, and a BA in post-colonial literature and creative writing from Hampshire College. Her writing has appeared in various journals, including The New Yorker, The New York Times, The Paris Review, and Transition . Lewis also has a band with Vijay Iyer, Julie Mehretu, and Jeffrey Ziegler. Their EP/LP, Archive of Desire , will be released next year, in 2027. Lewis collaborates with artists regularly, most recently: Alice Diop, Julie Mehretu, Lorna Simpson, Glenn Ligon, and composer Paola Prestini. A founding member of Julie Mehretu’s African Film and Media Arts Collective, Lewis’s video installations have been exhibited domestically and abroad, most recently at the Palazzo Grassi for the Venice Biennale. Forthcoming exhibitions will premiere next year at NY Public Library’s Schomburg Center Research in Black Culture, and Zeitz MoCAA in Capetown. A new opera, in collaboration with Paola Prestini and Ava DuVernay will premiere at Spoleto and NY PublicTheater in 2028. description: This conference will host conversations from a wide variety of disciplines and geographical areas around recovering the subjective experience of historically marginalized peoples. The problem of how to write about the historically marginalized — the enslaved, the illiterate, the imprisoned — has been the subject of innovative historiographical and cultural work globally in the last half century. Marxist historiographical approaches by E.P Thompson or the Indian Subaltern Studies school attempted to recover working and peasant class histories that were never written down. More recently, US Black studies has grappled with the impossibility of recovering experience of the enslaved. Most famously, Saidiya Hartman’s interventions advance imaginative aspects of recovery. Thinking beyond the strict remits of history as a discipline, she has emphasized the place of both speculation and active imagination in thinking through the impossibility of knowing much about lives deemed ‘unimportant’. So far, these area studies have had very little correspondence with each other. This conference will address this issue by bringing together scholarship working in different geographies and disciplines to discuss the global significance of the archival gap, share methodologies and insights, and collaborate on future scholarly output. Date: Thursday February 18, 2027 Time : 9:00am-6:30pm PST Location : Stanford Department of African and African American Studies, Building 80 (Main Quad) Auditorium Session details are forthcoming. description: How Climate Shocks Produce Armed Rebellion: The 1970 Bhola Cyclone and the Birth of Bangladesh Why do climate shocks produce conflict (Hsiang et al., 2013)? We study the 1970 Bhola cyclone in East Pakistan, one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history, which killed an estimated 350,000 people. Using satellite imagery, archival records, electoral returns, and insurgent biographies, we show that cyclone exposure amplified pre-existing separatist sentiment at the ballot box and increased citizens’ subsequent participation in guerrilla warfare against the state. Our estimates imply that exposure to the cyclone’s devastation induced an additional 48,613 insurgents to join the guerrilla war effort. Effects are larger in areas with pre-existing political and economic grievances and weaker relief provision. Our analysis reveals the step-by-step mechanisms through which environmental shocks can produce conflict: they shift voting behavior, expose state indifference, and convert grievance into armed mobilization. Bio Ahmed Mushfiq Mobarak is the Jerome Kasoff ’54 Professor of Management and Economics at Yale University with concurrent appointments in the School of Management and in the Department of Economics (Faculty of Arts and Sciences). Mobarak is the founder and faculty director of the Yale Research Initiative on Innovation and Scale (Y-RISE) . https://faculty.som.yale.edu/mushfiqmobarak/

description: Join Maggie Dethloff, Assistant Curator of Photography and New Media, on this special tour of California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area . RSVP here . How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present. The exhibition traces a series of interconnected currents — ecological, infrastructural, technological, personal, creative, and political — that have shaped both artistic production and everyday life in Northern California. Arranged thematically across time and media, California Current places historical works in conversation with contemporary ones, emphasizing both continuity and change. Together, they ask: What has drawn so many people to this region? What has allowed communities and creative practices to take root here? And what continues to keep so many of us — despite the Bay Area’s contradictions, pressures, and constant reinvention — deeply connected to this place? Presented as part of the Further Triennial, this exhibition features works by artists Pacita Abad, Saif Azzuz (Libyan-Yurok), Robert Bechtle, Bernice Bing, Kota Ezawa, L. description: Abstract: With its abundance of murals, paintings, sculptures, and ritual objects, Bhutan's material record remains remarkably intact. Yet it also remains significantly understudied, especially when compared to its cultural neighbors, Nepal and Tibet. Housed in a 17th century watchtower-fortress (Ta Dzong), the National Museum of Bhutan is frequently on the itineraries of tourists and scholars, however, many of the institution's most remarkable works are rarely, if ever, on view. This presentation draws from a two-year stay with the National Museum and a larger research project to compile the first art history of Bhutan. The talk will examine thangka from the collection–situating them in local and regional histories, delineating their distinctive aesthetic qualities, and addressing their broader socio-political contexts and meanings–with the aim of increasing recognition and appreciation of Bhutan's artistic heritage. Bio: Ariana is an art historian with expertise in Bhutan and the broader Himalaya. As part of her stay with the National Museum of Bhutan, she co-authored and edited Artful Contemplation , the institution's first catalog of the collection. Ariana's current research examines the workshops, patrons, and artists who made significant contributions to Bhutanese art history, which are the focus of a volume in progress. A two-time Fulbright U.S. Scholar to Bhutan, Ariana has worked with a range of institutions, including the Royal University, the Zhung Dratshang Preservation and Antiquities Center, and the National Library and Archives.
title: Ariana Maki: "Inside Ta Dzong: Bhutanese Art and History through the National Museum Collection"

description: Abstract: Buddhist traditions the world over have attended to the difficulties of giving birth. Early Chinese Buddhism offered expecting mothers a host of measures, including techniques to vanquish fear, exhortations to act morally, sacred syllables for chanting, special talismans to wear, deities offering protection, and merit-making rituals dedicated to a happy birth. After surveying Chinese Buddhist approaches to childbirth, this talk focuses on quotidian rituals that assigned merit to the safety of mothers and newborns. It draws on 20 handwritten liturgies from northwest China in the ninth and 10th centuries used by monks who provided ritual services to local families. The talk discusses concepts of illness and health, women’s medicine, the dynamics of Buddhist ritual, notions of karma and merit, and the interplay between childbirth, rebirth, and enlightenment. Bio: Stephen F. Teiser is D.T. Suzuki Professor in Buddhist Studies and Professor of Religion, Emeritus, Princeton University. His work concentrates on Chinese texts as well as artistic and material evidence from the silk road, reflecting on the interaction between Buddhism and local traditions. His monographs include The Ghost Festival in Medieval China (1988), The Scripture on the Ten Kings and the Making of Purgatory in Chinese Buddhism (1994), Reinventing the Wheel: Paintings of Rebirth in Medieval Buddhist Temples (2006), and Yili yu fojiao yanjiu (Ritual and the Study of Buddhism) (2022).
title: Stephen Teiser: "Merit for Mothers: Childbirth Rituals in Early Chinese Buddhism"

description: Abstract: Tibetan writers of kāvya -style poetry exploited the structured flexibility of the medium to praise the heroes and ideals of Buddhist tradition, to innovate in both literary form and practices of thought, and at times even to transgress the strictures implicit in other genres of Buddhist literature. This talk explores the popular genre of single verses intended to illustrate the poetic features described in Daṇḍin's Mirror of Poetry, and suggests that kāvya poetry was an important space in elite literature where pre-modern Tibetan writers could openly push the boundaries of Buddhist language, thought, and feeling. Bio: Kurtis Schaeffer is a student of Buddhist literature in Tibet and the Himalayas. He is the translator of The Life of the Buddha (2014) and Buddhist Meditation: Classic Teachings from Tibet (2024), both from Penguin Classics, and the author of Himalayan Hermitess (2004), The Culture of the Book in Tibet (2009), and other books. He is the Frances Myers Ball Professor in the Department of Religious Studies at the University of Virginia.

description: Join us for an afternoon of artmaking with Saif Azzuz, 2026-27 Doerr Visiting Artist, and cultural fire practitioner Elizabeth Azzuz. In this all ages, family friendly workshop, the Azzuzs will share the significance of cultural fire, or prescribed burns led by Indigenous practitioners to steward healthy ecosystems. Participants will create connections between native flora and fauna, and make pigments and drawings with charcoal from cultural fire burns. This program takes place on the O’Donohue Family Stanford Educational Farm at 555 Fremont Road, Stanford, CA, and is presented in conjunction with the Further Triennial exhibition California Current, on view at the Cantor from October 29, 2026 through 2028, which looks at the ecological, infrastructural, personal, creative, and activist networks that shape life in the region. Visit California Current to see works by Azzuz, which include charcoal drawings made from similar processes. All public programs at the Cantor Arts Center are always free! Space for this program is limited; advance registration is recommended. RSVP here . About the Presenters Saif Azzuz (b. 1987, born in Eureka, CA) is a Libyan-Yurok artist who resides in Pacifica, CA. He received a Bachelor’s Degree in Painting and Drawing from the California College of the Arts in 2013. Working in painting, sculpture and installation, Azzuz’s work reimagines and examines our relationships to nature, privatization and commodification. The use of different mediums allows Azzuz to explore and question complex and often conflicting histories and social contexts of materials, weaving in untold narratives. His work re­flects on the resilience of ecologies, first peoples and our collective need to view nature as an extension of us, in opposition to frameworks that view nature as a resource to be extracted. Elizabeth Azzuz is an enrolled member of the Yurok Tribe from the village of Weitchpec in Northern California, and a descendant of the Karuk Tribe, from the Village of Katamiin in Somes Bar. She is the Director of Traditional Fire for the Cultural Fire Management Council, and the treasurer to the Board of CFMC. She is also the Treasurer to the Indigenous Stewardship Network, and a member of the Indigenous Peoples Burning Network with the Nature Conservancy. Photos taken by Chris Grunder. Courtesy of the Artist and Anthony Meier Gallery. ​ ________ Directions & Parking The O'Donohue Family Stanford Educational Farm is located at 555 Fremont Road, Stanford. Free weekend parking is available in the Searsville Lot (Lot 22) at 190 Searsville Rd, directly adjacent to the farm (Stanford "A" and "C" permit spaces are free on Saturdays; just be sure to avoid 24/7 reserved spots). The best way to enter the farm is through the pedestrian gate located about halfway down the north pathway directly bordering the Searsville Lot. Address: 555 Fremont Road Stanford, Ca 94305 or 175 Electioneer Road Stanford, CA 94305 (please note the gate on Electioneer Rd. is often locked) Entrance: The best place to enter the farm is from the north gate along Searsville Lot (190 Searsville Rd. or L-22 parking lot) entrance. Accessibility Information or Requests Cantor Arts Center at Stanford University is committed to ensuring our programs are accessible to everyone. To request access information and/or accommodations for this event, please complete this form at least one week prior to the event: museum.stanford.edu/access . For questions, please contact disability.access@stanford.edu or Kwang-Mi Ro, kwangmi8@stanford.edu , (650) 723-3469.
